generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the cycle shows up across a whole module and beyond it: what you learn shapes how you approach the assessment, the assessment produces feedback, and the feedback, once you use it, changes how you learn next time. Seeing a single piece of work as one turn of that cycle, rather than a one-off, is what lets each assignment build on the last instead of starting from scratch.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students finish a module with the same comment on their final essay: a solid summary, but you needed to take more of a position of your own.

Student A treats learning, assessment and feedback as three things that happen and then end. The module is over and the mark is in, so the comment is read once and filed away. Nothing about it changes how Student A approaches the next module, and when the next essay comes back the same comment is there again: the cycle has simply repeated.

Student B treats the same comment as the start of the next round rather than the end of this one. It becomes something to act on: Student B plans the next essay around taking a clear position, and carries that into how the new material is read and revised from the outset. The next piece of work takes a position, and it is stronger, because the feedback fed back into the learning.

Both got the same comment. Only Student B treated the three as one cycle, letting feedback feed the next round of learning. That is what connects them, and it is what turns each piece of work into the start of the next improvement rather than a repeat of the last mistake.
generatedProse.summary: Learning, assessment and feedback are easiest to deal with one at a time, but they work as one connected cycle, where each part feeds the next and the whole comes round again. You can now show how they connect rather than stand alone, and recognise that cycle in your own experience of a module. Seeing the loop is what lets you carry effort from one part into the others, so that each piece of work becomes the start of the next improvement rather than a repeat of the last.

check.body: A student does well in one essay, reads the feedback, and uses it to plan the next essay, which comes back stronger. Which part of the learning, assessment and feedback cycle did using that feedback feed back into?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first essay, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next essay.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using feedback to plan the next piece of work feeds it straight back into your learning, closing the loop and starting the next round stronger. That is the cycle working as it should.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student did with the feedback, and what improved as a result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay was stronger. The mark on the first essay cannot change, but the feedback still shapes what comes next.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
